items.prompt: What happened to the liquid water in the puddle as the sun warmed it?
choices: It changed into tiny drops that floated up on the wind
It changed into an invisible gas called water vapor
It changed into runoff and was used up
It changed into cold air that rose high above the ground
items.why: The source says the sun's energy warmed the puddle and the liquid water slowly changed into an invisible gas called water vapor. Vapor is a gas, not drops; runoff flows and nothing is used up; water does not become air.

items.prompt: Which list names only kinds of precipitation?
choices: Rain, dust and hail
Snow, sleet and water vapor
Rain, clouds and sleet
Snow, sleet and hail
items.why: The source names rain, snow, sleet and hail as precipitation. Dust, water vapor and clouds are not water falling from clouds.

choices: The change from a gas to a liquid
The change from a liquid to a gas
The fall of water from clouds
The flow of water downhill over the ground
items.why: The source: this change from gas to liquid is called condensation. Liquid to gas is evaporation, falling water is precipitation, flowing water is runoff.

items.prompt: What is a cloud made of?
choices: Invisible water vapor rising with warm air
Bits of dust held up by cold air
Billions of tiny drops of liquid water gathered around bits of dust
Heavy drops that are falling to the ground
items.why: The source: the drops gather around bits of dust, and billions of them together form a cloud. Vapor is invisible and not yet a cloud; dust alone is not a cloud; heavy falling drops are precipitation.

items.prompt: On a humid day, a cold glass of water gets wet on the outside. A glass of warm water beside it stays dry. What best explains the difference?
choices: The water inside the cold glass is heavier, so it soaks out through the sides to the outside
The air around the warm glass has no water vapor in it
Evaporation is faster on the cold glass, so more water shows up on it
Only the cold glass cools the water vapor in the air enough to turn it to liquid
items.why: Level 3 push: a less friendly case (a warm glass beside the cold one) and a reason to give. The source: water vapor in the air touches the cold glass and turns to liquid, and vapor changes to liquid when it cools. The water comes from the air, not through the glass; both glasses sit in the same humid air; evaporation is liquid to gas and is faster when warm.

items.prompt: Why do the drops in a cloud finally fall?
choices: They join and grow too heavy for the air
They cool and change from a gas into a liquid
They pick up dust in the air, which pulls them down
They are warmed by the sun and change into water vapor
items.why: The source: the drops bump into each other and join, and when they grow too heavy for the air to hold up, they fall. Cooling into liquid is how the drops first form; dust is what they gather around; warming into vapor is evaporation.

items.prompt: Rain lands on a hillside. Which two things does the passage say can happen to that water on the ground?
choices: It soaks into the soil or rises as tiny liquid drops
It runs into plant roots or is used up by the soil
It soaks into the soil or runs downhill as runoff
It runs downhill as runoff or gathers around dust
items.why: The source: some water soaks into the soil, and some runs downhill over the surface as runoff. Water rises as vapor, not drops; none is used up; drops gather around dust in the air, not on the ground.

items.prompt: A student says, "The puddle's water is gone for good." Which idea from the passage best shows the student is wrong?
choices: The puddle's water soaked into the soil, so it stays in the schoolyard
The puddle's water became vapor, and the same water keeps moving through the cycle; none is used up
The puddle's water turned into a gas, and a gas cannot turn back into a liquid
New water is made in clouds to take the place of water that is used up
items.why: Level 3 push: a reason to give. The source: the water did not vanish, it evaporated; the same water keeps moving through the steps, no new water is made and none is used up. The puddle evaporated rather than soaked in; vapor does change back to liquid; no new water is made.

items.prompt: After the same storm, two puddles of the same size sit in two different towns. One is gone in a day. The other lasts four days. What was most likely true where the puddle lasted longer?
choices: The air was cool and still
The air was warm and the wind blew
The air was colder high above the ground
The sun gave the puddle more energy
items.why: Level 3 push: the unknown in a new place (the result is given and the cause is asked). The source: evaporation is slower when it is cool and still. Warm, windy air and more sun energy make it faster; colder air high up is about clouds forming, not the puddle.

items.prompt: Why do clouds form high above the ground?
choices: Water vapor is too heavy for the air near the ground to hold up
The air high up is warmer, so the liquid water changes to an invisible gas there
The air high up is colder, so the vapor cools and changes to liquid drops
The air high up is windier, so evaporation happens faster there
items.why: Level 3 push: a reason to give, with the term not named. The source: high above the ground the air is colder, and when water vapor cools it changes back into tiny drops of liquid water. Vapor rises with warm air; the high air is colder, not warmer; evaporation makes vapor, not clouds.
